\chapter{Long, Moving and Curled}
\label{ch:ka-chihnegaLu}
\hlchaptermodality{79}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can read the three vowel signs this book had never named, and tell Kannada's two n letters and three s letters apart on the page.}

From cold: name the three signs and say what each does to the consonant under it, then sort \kn{ನ} against \kn{ಣ} and \kn{ಸ}, \kn{ಶ}, \kn{ಷ} by where the tongue sits.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ī]{\kn{◌ೀ} — the long one, on the sign you already read}

\label{lesson:KA-S161-vowel-sign-ii}



\begin{quote}
You say \emph{nīnu} and \emph{nīvu} every time you address somebody. The mark that makes that \emph{i} long is the one you have never been shown.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ೀ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ೀ}} — \emph{ī}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign} — it cannot stand alone, it rides on a consonant and changes the vowel that consonant carries.

Set it beside the short one you have read since chapter four:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{short} & \textbf{long} \\
\midrule
\kn{ಿ} — \emph{i} & \kn{ೀ} — \emph{ī} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{This is the most-used character in this book that nothing has taught.} It is in the word for \emph{you}, in the colour blue, and in the polite verb ending you use whenever you ask somebody how they are.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀನು} / \kn{ನೀವು}} \emph{nīnu / nīvu} — you, familiar and respectful
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀಲಿ}} \emph{nīli} — blue
  \item \textbf{\kn{ನೀವು} \kn{ಹೇಗಿದ್ದೀರಾ}?} \emph{nīvu hēgiddīrā?} — how are you? — and the ending carries it twice
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{◌ೀ}}
Put your pen on \kn{◌ೀ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

\begin{quote}
This book does not yet tell you \textbf{where to start the character or which way to travel}. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words, and find \kn{◌ೀ} in each
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನೀನು}  ·  \kn{ನೀಲಿ}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{◌ೀ} three times, saying \emph{ī} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this book and find \kn{◌ೀ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which mark is this — \kn{◌ೀ}? What does it do to the consonant under it? (\textbf{Makes its vowel a long \emph{ī}}.) Which word for \emph{you} carries it? (\textbf{Both of them}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[ai]{\kn{◌ೈ} — the sign for the vowel that moves}

\label{lesson:KA-S162-vowel-sign-ai}



\begin{quote}
A chapter ago you wrote \textbf{\kn{ಐ}}, the letter for \emph{ai}. Here is the same vowel when a consonant is carrying it.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ೈ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ೈ}} — \emph{ai}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign} — it cannot stand alone, it rides on a consonant and changes the vowel that consonant carries.

\textbf{\kn{ಐ}} and \textbf{\kn{◌ೈ}} are one vowel with two jobs. The letter opens a word; the sign sits on a consonant inside one. You met the pair idea with every other vowel in this script, and this is the last of them to arrive.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕ}} plus \textbf{\kn{◌ೈ}} gives \textbf{\kn{ಕೈ}} — \emph{kai}, a hand
\end{itemize}

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ತಲೆ} \kn{ಕೈ}} \emph{tale kai} — head and hand
  \item \textbf{\kn{ವೈದ್ಯ}} \emph{vaidya} — a doctor
  \item \textbf{\kn{ರೈತ}} \emph{raita} — a farmer
\end{itemize}

\section[au]{\kn{◌ೌ} — the mark in the third word you learned}

\label{lesson:KA-S163-vowel-sign-au}



\begin{quote}
Say yes in Kannada. That word has carried today's mark since chapter one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{◌ೌ}}
\textbf{\kn{◌ೌ}} — \emph{au}.

It is a \textbf{vowel sign} — it cannot stand alone, it rides on a consonant and changes the vowel that consonant carries.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹ}} plus \textbf{\kn{◌ೌ}} gives \textbf{\kn{ಹೌ}} — the first syllable of \emph{haudu}
\end{itemize}

Like \emph{ai}, this vowel \textbf{moves while you say it}: it starts low and slides toward \emph{u}. Two sounds in one mark, which is what the romanization's two letters are showing.

Every vowel in this script has two forms — a letter for the front of a word, a sign for inside one. This one's letter form is the single independent vowel whose stroke order this project has no source for, so chapter 78 stopped short of it. \textbf{The sign is what a reader actually meets on these pages}, and it is the form this book can hand over honestly.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಹೌದು}} \emph{haudu} — yes
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಗೌರವ}} \emph{gaurava} — respect
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸೌಜನ್ಯ}} \emph{saujanya} — courtesy
\end{itemize}

\section[ṇa]{\kn{ಣ} — the n with the tongue curled back}

\label{lesson:KA-S164-letter-nna}



\begin{quote}
Say the word for an eye. There are two n-sounds in Kannada and that word has the one you have never been shown.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಣ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಣ}} — \emph{ṇa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṇ}, it is \textbf{ṇa}.

Kannada keeps \textbf{two different n letters} apart on the page, and English marks neither.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{romanized} & \textbf{where the tongue goes} \\
\midrule
\kn{ನ} & \emph{na} & tip behind the teeth \\
\kn{ಣ} & \emph{ṇa} & curled back along the roof \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

You have read \textbf{\kn{ನ}} since the first chapter. \textbf{\kn{ಣ}} is the same sound made further back, with the tongue curled — the position you already use for \textbf{\kn{ಟ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಡ}}.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}} \emph{kaṇṇu} — an eye
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಸಿಗೋಣ}} \emph{sigōṇa} — let us meet, inside the farewell
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಖಂಡಿತ}} \emph{khaṇḍita} — certainly
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \kn{ಣ}}
Put your pen on \kn{ಣ} and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright

\end{itemize}

\end{quote}

  \item \emph{Trace it:} \kn{ಣ} three times, saying \emph{ṇa} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this book and find \kn{ಣ} once more

\section[śa]{\kn{ಶ} — the letter every greeting starts with}

\label{lesson:KA-S165-letter-sha}



\begin{quote}
Say good morning, good evening and good night. All three begin on today's character.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಶ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಶ}} — \emph{śa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ś}, it is \textbf{śa}.

Every time-of-day greeting in this book opens with \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ}} \emph{śubha}, “auspicious” — and that word begins on \kn{ಶ}.

Kannada prints \textbf{three separate s letters}, and you have had only one of them. \kn{ಸ} you met in chapter twelve; \kn{ಶ} is here; \kn{ಷ} is on the next page.

You already say these:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ರಾತ್ರಿ}} \emph{śubha rātri} — good night
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ}} \emph{śubhōdaya} — good morning
  \item \textbf{\kn{ಶುಭ} \kn{ಸಂಜೆ}} \emph{śubha sañje} — good evening
\end{itemize}

\section[ṣa]{\kn{ಷ} — the third s, and the last one}

\label{lesson:KA-S166-letter-ssa}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: \kn{ಶ}, and \kn{ಸ} from chapter twelve. Today's is the third and final s-shape.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \kn{ಷ}}
\textbf{\kn{ಷ}} — \emph{ṣa}.

It is a \textbf{consonant}, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an \emph{a} already in it. So it is not \emph{ṣ}, it is \textbf{ṣa}.

Now you have the whole set:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{letter} & \textbf{romanized} & \textbf{where the tongue goes} \\
\midrule
\kn{ಸ} & \emph{sa} & tip behind the teeth \\
\kn{ಶ} & \emph{śa} & flat against the front of the roof \\
\kn{ಷ} & \emph{ṣa} & curled back along the roof \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\kn{ಷ} curls back in the same place as \kn{ಣ}.} That is the one position this script keeps naming and English never marks, and you have now met it on an n and on an s.

Look at \textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}}: it opens on \kn{ಸ} and closes on \kn{ಷ}. Until today you could read one end of that word and not the other.

\raggedright

\section[chihnegaLu mattu sa-galu]{(\kn{ೀ} \kn{ೈ} \kn{ೌ} \kn{ಣ} \kn{ಶ} \kn{ಷ}) — six characters, two ideas}

\label{lesson:KA-R79-signs-and-sibilants}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{you} the respectful way, and say yes. Name the mark each of those words carries.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script: six shapes, two ideas}
\textbf{One — a vowel can be long, or it can move.} Three signs, and none of them can stand on its own:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{sign} & \textbf{sound} & \textbf{met in} \\
\midrule
\kn{◌ೀ} & \emph{ī} & \kn{ನೀವು} — you \\
\kn{◌ೈ} & \emph{ai} & \kn{ಕೈ} — a hand \\
\kn{◌ೌ} & \emph{au} & \kn{ಹೌದು} — yes \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Two — the tongue can curl back}, and Kannada writes that position where English marks nothing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{flat} & \textbf{curled} \\
\midrule
\kn{ನ} \emph{na} & \kn{ಣ} \emph{ṇa} \\
\kn{ಸ} \emph{sa} & \kn{ಷ} \emph{ṣa} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{\kn{ಶ}} \emph{śa} is the third s — flat against the front of the roof. One set of three where English has a single letter, and the word \textbf{\kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}} uses two of them, one at each end.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at these words and name every character in them
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\kn{ನೀವು}  ·  \kn{ಹೌದು}  ·  \kn{ಸಂತೋಷ}  ·  \kn{ಶುಭೋದಯ}  ·  \kn{ಕಣ್ಣು}
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which two of the six put your tongue in the curled-back position
  \item which of the three signs is a vowel that moves while you say it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which sign makes an \emph{i} long? (\textbf{\kn{◌ೀ}}.) Which two characters are made with the tongue curled back? (\textbf{\kn{ಣ}} and \textbf{\kn{ಷ}}.) How many s letters does Kannada print? (\textbf{Three} — \kn{ಸ}, \kn{ಶ}, \kn{ಷ}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
